subject: AI & Agents
title: The Black Box Problem
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Black Box Problem.

hook.text: An AI denies your loan. You ask why. Nobody — not even the developers — can give you a clear answer.

buildup.text: Deep neural networks process data through millions of interconnected parameters.

discovery.text: The network's reasoning is distributed across all those parameters. No single part holds the 'reason.'

twist.text: Explainable AI (XAI) research creates approximations, but true transparency remains elusive.

climax.text: The EU's AI Act now requires explanations for high-stakes AI decisions. The technology isn't fully ready.

punchline.text: A decision without an explanation isn't accountability. It's authority.

quiz.question: Why is the 'black box' problem concerning for AI decisions?
options: Nobody can clearly explain why the AI made a specific decision
The physical hardware is literally painted black

details.summary: Many AI models operate as black boxes — they produce outputs without explaining their reasoning. Understanding exactly why a model made a specific decision is often technically impossible.
details.whyItMatters: Black box AI makes accountability difficult. When a model denies a loan or diagnoses a disease, affected people deserve to understand why, making explainability a rights issue.
takeaways: Complex AI models process decisions through billions of parameters
Even developers often cannot explain specific model outputs
Explainable AI is a growing research and regulatory priority

faq.question: Why can't we open up AI models to see how they decide?
faq.answer: Neural networks contain millions to billions of parameters interacting in complex ways. While we can examine individual weights, the emergent decision logic is too complex for human interpretation.

faq.question: Are there regulations requiring AI explainability?
faq.answer: GDPR provides a right to explanation for automated decisions. The EU AI Act requires transparency for high-risk systems. More jurisdictions are developing similar requirements.
